source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC3532875 (author manuscript of Drug Alcohol Depend 2007;86:1-21), body read in full in my own browser tab (abstract, sections 1 to 6, acknowledgements, footnotes); no tables or figures in the body; the online supplementary table of the 1975-2005 search results was not read (supplements are not read in this round); reference list not needed for the claims' figures

claims.overstatement: The claim says Greenfield et al. call faster progression in women one of the most reproducible findings. They do not, exactly. The Introduction's first sentence gives that label to women's heightened vulnerability to the adverse medical and social consequences of use. The next sentence states faster progression as established, for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence, citing six studies. Suggested wording: 'states it as established, beside calling women's vulnerability to adverse consequences one of the most reproducible findings'. Also, this review's list is alcohol, opioid (not split into prescription and heroin) and cannabis, with no cocaine and no heroin exception; the claim's list comes from McHugh et al. And this review does not call its evidence mostly treatment samples: one of the six sources is Dawson (1996), a general-population survey.
claims.note: Internal tension in the source. The Introduction cites Dawson (1996) for women advancing faster from use to first treatment. Section 2.3 describes the same study as finding no gender difference in treatment entry for 8 years after onset and men 13–20% more likely to enter treatment between 8 and 25 years. Section 2.3 also cites clinical studies for women's shorter interval from regular use to treatment entry, then says clinical studies found little difference in the likelihood or rate of treatment entry. The review was searched systematically (Medline and PsycInfo, 1975–September 2005) but the studies were not formally appraised, and the Introduction's progression statement gives no design, timing measure or adjustment.

anchors.locator: 1. Introduction, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: First sentence: among the most reproducible findings is women's heightened vulnerability to the adverse medical and social consequences of use. Second sentence: for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence, women advance more rapidly from use to regular use to first treatment than men (Dawson 1996; Hernandez-Avila 2004; Johnson 2005; Orford & Keddie 1985; Piazza 1989; Randall 1999). Symptom severity at treatment entry is said to be equal despite fewer years of use, and age at first use roughly equal in younger cohorts.

anchors.locator: 2. Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry › 2.3 Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry and Ever Receiving Treatment, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Women's shorter interval from regular drug use to treatment entry is cited from clinical studies (Grella 1999; Hernandez-Avila 2004; McCance 1999). Several clinical studies are then said to find little difference between women and men in the likelihood or rate of treatment entry (Green 2002; Timko 2002).

anchors.locator: 2. Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry › 2.3 Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry and Ever Receiving Treatment, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Dawson (1996), one of the Introduction's six sources for faster progression, is described here as a population survey (NLAES 1992, n = 7,359) with no gender difference in treatment entry up to 8 years after onset, men 13–20% more likely to start treatment between 8 and 25 years, and lower lifetime treatment in women (23% vs 15.1%).

anchors.locator: 1. Introduction › 1.1 Search Method, 1st paragraph; 1.2 Search Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Medline and PsycInfo were searched for January 1975 to September 2005, English only, all substances except nicotine. 2,474 plus 636 records gave 280 relevant articles, screened by three authors; 11.8% were randomized trials. No appraisal tool is described.

claims.note: Every Greenfield figure in the statement and magnitude checks. Dawson (1996): 7,359 NLAES respondents with alcohol abuse or dependence; 23% of men vs 15.1% of women ever treated, counting physician, counsellor, AA, other professional or treatment facility; cumulative probability by 30 years .424 vs .356; no difference up to 8 years; men 13–20% more likely between 8 and 25 years; no difference in the most severe; men-to-women ratio 1.75:1 with one symptom to 1.24:1 with 15 symptoms (among the less severely affected). Wu & Ringwalt (1999 survey, n = 32,628): past-year alcohol treatment 12.5% vs 12.1%. Mojtabai (2002 NSDUH): gender not significant for past-year use of substance abuse services. Ratios 3.3:1 vs 2.7:1 (1991) and 2.3:1 (2002) vs 1.9:1 and 1.5:1 (2003). Women more often in non-specialty, especially mental-health, settings (Weisner & Schmidt 1992). Barriers: pregnancy, custody, prosecution, childcare, co-occurring disorders, stigma. Two small qualifications. In the same 1999 survey, specialty and non-specialty use did not differ by gender (5.7% vs 4.3%; 6.8% vs 7.7%). The review describes Dawson only as a retrospective cohort, without adjustment, and the claim says so correctly.

anchors.locator: 2. Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry › 2.3 Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry and Ever Receiving Treatment, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Dawson (1996): retrospective cohort of 7,359 respondents with alcohol abuse or dependence from the population-based 1992 NLAES. Ever treated, by a physician, counsellor, AA, other professional or treatment facility: men 23%, women 15.1%. Cumulative conditional probability of treatment by 30 years after onset .424 in men vs .356 in women. No gender difference up to 8 years after onset; between 8 and 25 years men were 13%–20% more likely to start treatment.

anchors.locator: 2. Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry › 2.3 Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry and Ever Receiving Treatment, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The 8-year finding is said to agree with Timko 2005 and with Wu & Ringwalt's past-year result. In the most severe dependence there was no gender difference; among the less severely affected, the men-to-women ratio of treatment entry ranged from 1.75:1 (one symptom) to 1.24:1 (15 symptoms).

anchors.locator: 2. Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry › 2.3 Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry and Ever Receiving Treatment, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 1999 US National Household Survey (n = 32,628; Wu & Ringwalt 2004). Among people who drank, men to women with alcohol dependence was 1.7:1. Past-year alcohol treatment among people with dependence was 12.5% in women vs 12.1% in men, with no difference in specialty (5.7% vs 4.3%) or non-specialty (6.8% vs 7.7%) services. Timko 2005 followed 230 women and 236 men, initially untreated, for 8 years: no difference in the type of services received; women had longer professional treatment in the first year.

anchors.locator: 2. Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry › 2.3 Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry and Ever Receiving Treatment, 4th and 5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: In the 2002 NSDUH (Mojtabai 2005), substance type was related to past-year treatment entry but gender, race/ethnicity and insurance did not significantly affect use of substance abuse services. A three-country survey (Kessler 2001) found no gender difference in ever seeking help, but defined help-seeking broadly (telling a professional or attending self-help; 50–85% had done so).

anchors.locator: 2. Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry › 2.1 Gender Disparities among Participants in Substance Abuse Treatment, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Men to women: 3.3:1 in US alcohol treatment facilities in 1991 (Dawson 1996), against an estimated 2.7:1 for alcohol use disorders in the population (Grant 1994). 2.3:1 in US treatment facilities in 2002, against 2003 NSDUH past-year ratios of 1.9:1 for alcohol dependence and 1.5:1 for illicit drug dependence. Australia: 2:1 for high-risk drinking in the population against 3:1 to 10:1 in alcohol treatment services.

anchors.locator: 2. Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry › 2.2 Gender Disparities in Choice of Treatment Service Sectors, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Women with problem drinking were more likely than men to seek care in non-alcohol-specific settings, especially mental-health services (Weisner & Schmidt 1992); men were less likely to use mental-health, but not substance abuse, services (Mojtabai 2005).

anchors.locator: 2. Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry › 2.4 Specific Barriers to Treatment Entry for Women, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Barriers documented for women, mostly cited from earlier reviews: pregnancy and lack of services for pregnant women; fear of losing custody or of prosecution; childcare responsibilities without childcare; co-occurring mood, eating, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorders; trauma histories; lack of family or partner support; greater stigma.

anchors.locator: 2. Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry › 2.7 Summary, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Studies with short follow-up after onset (1–8 years) or broad definitions found no gender difference in treatment entry. Population surveys covering more than 8 years show a lower lifetime probability of alcohol treatment in women (Dawson 1996). Women are less likely over the lifetime to enter treatment and more likely to seek it in non-specialty settings.

claims.overstatement: Three omissions make the claim's account slightly one-sided. (1) The small clinical retention studies split 5 to 2 against women: five found women more likely to drop out, two found men more likely. 'Disagreed in both directions' is true but hides that balance. (2) Kaskutas et al. (2005): the women-only day programme did no worse than the two community mixed-gender programmes. Only the hospital-based programme, which cost twice as much per week, had higher abstinence, and the review concludes women may be equally well served by good mixed-gender and women-only day programmes. (3) In the older-adult study, women still had fewer heavy-drinking days (none vs an average of four in the past month) after the abstinence difference disappeared.
claims.note: All Greenfield figures check: 280 articles 1975–2005; 11.8% randomized trials (plus 7.9% non-randomized or quasi-experimental and 31.2% prospective cohorts); 10,010 patients in 96 programmes (11 US cities), men 20% less likely to stay at least 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; 26,047 patients in 87 Los Angeles programmes, women more likely to complete where differences appeared; 4,689 adults (1,239 women; ADSS 1996–1999), gender not associated with completion after adjustment; older adults 79.3% vs 54% abstinent at 6 months, not significant after controlling for length of stay. 'Where a difference appeared it more often favoured women' is the review's own reading (section 4.1, 2nd paragraph, 14 citations; section 6, 4th paragraph). The randomized women-only vs mixed-gender comparisons are Condelli 2000 (no difference in early attrition), Strantz & Welch 1995 (higher retention in the women-only day programme) and Kaskutas 2005, the only one on substance outcomes. The switch to gender-specific groups is Bride 2001 (no change in completion or retention). The review notes that retention and completion were defined in many ways.

anchors.locator: Abstract; 1. Introduction › 1.2 Search Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: 2,474 Medline and 636 PsycInfo records, screened by three authors, gave 280 relevant articles (1975–2005); 90% were from 1990 on, and 43.9% of those from 2000 on. 11.8% were randomized trials, 7.9% non-randomized or quasi-experimental, 31.2% prospective cohorts. No appraisal tool was used.

anchors.locator: 3. Characteristics Associated with Substance Abuse Treatment Retention and Completion, 1st paragraph (section introduction)
anchors.extracted: Up to 50% of patients drop out in the first month. Retention and completion are defined in diverse ways: sessions attended, days in treatment, length of stay, completion of sessions or goals. This makes studies hard to compare.

anchors.locator: 3. › 3.1 Gender Differences in Treatment Retention, 1st–4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Smaller clinical studies were inconsistent. Five found women more likely to drop out (e.g., Detroit, 1,804 men and 667 women, after adjustment; buprenorphine, 25% of women vs 13% of men early terminators). Two found women less likely to drop out (Los Angeles, 511; methamphetamine, 2,570). One was mixed (New Jersey, 1,573). Four found no difference; the 4th paragraph says three, then describes four.

anchors.locator: 3. › 3.1 Gender Differences in Treatment Retention, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Larger population-based samples converge on few or no gender differences in retention. Simpson 1997: 10,010 patients in 96 programmes in 11 US cities; the only gender difference was that men in outpatient drug-free care were 20% less likely than women to stay 90 days or more. Hser 2001: 26,047 patients in 87 Los Angeles programmes, with very few gender associations; where they existed, women were more likely to complete (360 days of methadone; 180 days outpatient drug-free).

anchors.locator: 3. › 3.1 Gender Differences in Treatment Retention, 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Alcohol and Drug Services Study (1996–1999, public and private facilities): 4,689 adults, 1,239 women. After controlling for client and facility characteristics, gender was not associated with completing planned treatment. Women-only facilities or childcare were not associated with completion among women.

anchors.locator: 4. Characteristics associated with Substance Abuse Treatment Outcomes in Women › 4.1 Substance Abuse Outcomes versus Predictors of Outcomes, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Many studies found few or no gender differences in outcome: DATOS across four modalities; Hser 2003 at one year; Green 2004; Greenfield 1998 (the reviewers' own); Alterman 2000; Foster 2000 at 12 weeks; a meta-analysis of seven brief-intervention studies (Ballesteros 2004). Predictors of outcome often differed by gender.

anchors.locator: 4. › 4.1 Substance Abuse Outcomes versus Predictors of Outcomes, 2nd–4th and 6th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: When gender differences were found, adult women generally had better outcomes (14 citations). Examples: cocaine inpatients, women more often abstinent at 6 months (Weiss 1997); methamphetamine, 567 women and 506 men, women improved more in family and medical domains (Hser 2005); randomized trial with 34 women and 29 men with crack cocaine dependence, longer abstinence in women (Henskens 2005); brief treatment, women improved more (Sanchez-Craig 1991); relapse outcomes better in women (Project MATCH aftercare arm: men had fewer abstinent days).

anchors.locator: 4. › 4.1 Substance Abuse Outcomes versus Predictors of Outcomes, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Older adults in outpatient alcohol treatment (Satre 2004): at 6 months, 79.3% of women vs 54% of men reported no alcohol or drugs in the past 30 days. The difference did not persist after controlling for longer length of stay. Women had eliminated heavy-drinking days, against an average of four in the past month for men.

anchors.locator: 5. Gender-Specific Versus Mixed-Gender Treatment Services › 5.2 Comparisons of Women-Only versus Mixed-Gender Treatment Settings, 1st–3rd and 6th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Few randomized trials compare women-only and mixed-gender settings. Condelli 2000: no difference in refusals or attrition in the first 25 days. Strantz & Welch 1995: retention higher in the women-only intensive day programme than in traditional outpatient care. Bride 2001, an agency switching to gender-specific groups: no difference in completion or retention. Kaskutas 2005, randomized: the only significant difference was higher total abstinence in a hospital-based mixed-gender programme (Minnesota model, medical staff, twice the cost per week) than in the women-only programme; there was no difference from two community mixed-gender programmes; the sample was small. The authors conclude women may be equally well served by either.

anchors.locator: 5. › 5.2 Comparisons of Women-Only versus Mixed-Gender Treatment Settings, 4th and 5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Non-randomized comparisons: Copeland 1993 (Australia) found no outcome difference, though the women-only unit took more complex patients. Grella 1999 found that women in publicly funded women-only residential programmes stayed more days and completed more often, despite more complex problems.

anchors.locator: 6. Summary of Findings and Implications for Research on Gender Differences and Substance Abuse Treatment Outcomes, 3rd, 4th and 6th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Gender is not necessarily a predictor of retention, completion or outcome once treatment begins. The older belief that women do worse is not substantiated, and several studies show better outcomes for women. Merely changing a programme from mixed-gender to women-only does not necessarily change outcomes; gender-specific programming helps only certain subgroups of women.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed as worded. The finding rightly does not say 'most reproducible'; see the interpretation-gap note for where the card does.
Minor: the review calls the source (Swift & Copeland 1996) a quasi-experimental study of women's treatment needs, with percentages of the women surveyed.

risk_of_bias.note: Some concerns is fair: two named databases, terms, dates, record counts and three screeners, but relevance as the only criterion and no appraisal. Overall equals the worst domain. For consistency: sc_mchugh_2018 rates its reuse of this search 'high', because databases and screening are not reported there.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is fair, but gap point (2) needs a correction. The Introduction does not call faster progression one of the most reproducible findings. That label goes to women's heightened vulnerability to adverse medical and social consequences; faster progression follows in the next sentence as an unlabelled statement of fact, which the paragraph later folds into 'this heightened vulnerability'. The same misreading appears in cl_gen_telescoping and in sc_keyes_2010's timeline entry for this review. The rest of point (2), Dawson (1996) pointing the other way, is confirmed.

missed: Section 5.2, 6th paragraph (Kaskutas et al. 2005): the women-only day programme did not differ from the two community-based mixed-gender programmes, and the authors conclude women may be equally well served by good mixed-gender and women-only day programmes. Key finding 12 gives only the hospital-programme difference.

Section 4.1, 5th paragraph (Satre 2004): after the abstinence difference disappeared with adjustment for length of stay, women still had no heavy-drinking days against an average of four in the past month for men.

Reporting issue, section 3.3, 2nd paragraph: the demonstration project (Roberts & Nishimoto 1996) is said to randomize women to a women-focused day programme or traditional outpatient care, but the completion comparison reported is against residential programmes. The description does not hang together and the finding should be taken from the primary paper.
